passage: The lights went out across the lane just as the shouting started outside Mr. Ansari's door. Naveen, twenty-five, saw torches and a knot of men in the dark, one of them yelling about what Mr. Ansari's family cooked. Naveen's heart pounded. He didn't shout back. He called down to his flatmate Sumit, "Get the other neighbours, quietly," and walked across in his slippers. "Uncle, I'm here," he said, standing beside the old man at the door. Mrs. Rao arrived with her torch, then two more families. The men saw a small crowd of neighbours and no fight. Naveen said calmly, "We know this house. Please go home." They muttered and left. Later Naveen rang the society secretary to report it, and the secretary promised to come in the morning with the guard and speak to everyone.

passage: Vishal noticed the folded note taped to Seema's door on Monday morning: "Your kind not welcome here." Seema, a Christian neighbour on the third floor who taught music at home, was standing in the corridor holding it, her jaw tight. Vishal, twenty-four, did not say "how awful" and walk on. He said, "May I stand with you for a minute? Shall we take this to the society secretary together?" They went down. The secretary, Mr. Batra, read the note twice. "This is not acceptable. I will put up a notice and ask the guard to keep watch after ten." Seema thanked him quietly. That evening Vishal knocked with a plate of pohe and asked if he could sit in on her Saturday music class; he had always wanted to learn the keys. She smiled for the first time that day.

qa.a: Vishal stayed with her and went with her to the society secretary, so the note was reported together and Mr. Batra promised a notice and a watch.

qa.a: At first Seema is hurt and shaken, with a tight jaw. Later she feels some comfort, since a neighbour offered company and the secretary took it seriously.

"Noor, open the door. It's Sarika from next door."
"...Sarika?"
"I saw what someone wrote on your gate. Are you okay?"
"My mother is crying. My brother wants to go and find who did it."
"Please don't let him. Let me come in."
"People are watching from the balconies."
"Let them watch me walk in, then. Here, I've brought tea."
"...Why are you doing this?"
"Because you watered my plants for a month when I was in hospital. And because nobody should come home to that."
"What do we do?"
"First, photos of the gate. Then I'll call the police station with you, and the society secretary. We'll write the complaint together."
"And the paint?"
"After the police see it, I'll help you scrub it off. Tomorrow I'll walk your mother to the market."
"...Thank you, Sarika."

qa.a: Sarika said, "Here, I've brought tea."

qa.a: Noor was frightened and unsure, with her mother crying and people watching from the balconies.

qa.q: How did Sarika show simple solidarity without stoking anger?
qa.a: She discouraged the brother from going after anyone, helped document and report it to the police and society, offered to help clean the gate and walk Noor's mother to market.

qa.q: How might the neighbours on the balconies see Sarika walking in?
qa.a: Some may feel uncomfortable, but seeing a neighbour stand openly beside Noor's family might make others braver to help too.

grounding: A young adult stands beside a neighbour of another faith after a hostile act, offering company and practical help without stoking anger.

subtype: Standing beside a neighbour under threat [Response]
passage:
I was the only young man on our lane who went to the Fernandes house that night, and I'm still not proud of how long it took me.
Someone had thrown stones at their windows after a rumour about "conversions." Mr. and Mrs. Fernandes are both in their seventies. I watched from my window for an hour, angry, wanting to post something furious online.
My friend Anirban called. "Kamal, stop typing. Just go there." So I went. Mrs. Fernandes opened the door with her hands shaking.
I didn't say much. I swept the glass off their veranda. Anirban came with cardboard to cover the windows. We called the police together and stayed until an officer came.
The next morning, two more neighbours brought breakfast. Looking back, the post I didn't send would have made more noise. Sweeping glass did more.

qa.q: What did Anirban bring to cover the windows?
qa.a: Anirban came with cardboard to cover the windows.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he watched from the window?
qa.a: Kamal felt angry and wanted to post something furious online, and now feels regret that it took him so long to go.

qa.q: Why was sweeping glass better than an angry post?
qa.a: Practical help and company protected the elderly couple and got the police involved, without stirring more anger that might make things worse.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Fernandes have felt when Kamal came to the door?
qa.a: She was frightened, with her hands shaking, and was likely relieved and comforted to have a neighbour beside her.

grounding: A young man chooses practical company and help for elderly neighbours of another faith after an attack, instead of stoking anger online.

Community centre coordinator's note, resident meeting, Sunday.
At today's meeting, several residents proposed banning the Rahmat family from holding Friday prayers in their own flat, saying it "draws outsiders." Voices rose. Mr. Rahmat stood at the back, silent.
Himani, 25, a tenant on the fourth floor, stood up. She said calmly, "They've prayed there for twelve years. Nobody complained until last month. I don't want our building to be the kind that does this." She did not accuse anyone by name. Then she walked to the back and stood beside Mr. Rahmat.
Karthik, from the second floor, came and stood with them. Then two more residents.
The proposal was dropped. After the meeting, I spoke with the Rahmat family, who said they felt shaken but supported, and I noted Himani's offer to walk Mrs. Rahmat to the bus each morning this week.

qa.q: How long had the Rahmat family prayed in their flat?
qa.a: They had prayed there for twelve years.

qa.q: What might Mr. Rahmat have been feeling standing silently at the back?
qa.a: He was probably anxious and humiliated, hearing neighbours propose to stop his family's prayers.

qa.q: What made Himani's response effective?
qa.a: She spoke calmly, without accusing anyone, then stood beside Mr. Rahmat, which encouraged Karthik and others to join and led to the proposal being dropped.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when he came to stand with them?
qa.a: Karthik may have felt encouraged and braver once Himani went first, choosing solidarity over staying quiet.

grounding: A coordinator's note records a young adult standing beside a neighbour of another faith facing hostility, offering company and a calm voice.

subtype: Standing beside a neighbour under threat [Response]
passage:
Kamal's diary. Friday, 11 pm.
Someone chalked an ugly line on Devika Aunty's gate this evening, about her temple bell being "noise". Two boys on a bike shouted it again at eight. She is seventy and lives alone since Uncle died. I went over with Ammi's biryani as an excuse and stayed till ten.
We scrubbed the gate together. I called the police helpline, and the station sent a constable, who took a photo and noted the bike's colour. I also wrote in our lane group: "Devika Aunty has lived here forty years. If you see anything, call me or the police." Six neighbours replied. Farhan offered to walk her to the market.
I wanted to hunt those boys down. I didn't write that in the group. Anger at them won't keep her safe; people at her gate will.
She rang her bell at nine like always. I heard it from my room.

qa.q: What did the constable do after arriving?
qa.a: The constable took a photo and noted the bike's colour.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling about the boys on the bike?
qa.a: Kamal felt angry enough to want to hunt them down, but chose to keep that anger out of the lane group.

qa.q: Why was Kamal's message to the lane group a wise step?
qa.a: It asked neighbours to watch out and to call the police, gathering company around Devika Aunty without stirring anger against anyone.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Devika Aunty to ring her bell at nine as usual?
qa.a: It suggests she felt steadier and less alone, safe enough to keep her own practice after neighbours stood by her.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who offers company, practical help and a calm public voice when an elderly neighbour of another faith faces hostility.
